planting.note: Plant divisions in sharply drained, humus-poor or lime-rich soil in rock crevices, old walls, or at the base of trees in partial shade; this calcicole fern resents heavy, wet garden soil and performs best where its roots can wedge into mortar joints or thin pockets of soil over rock.

directions: Welsh polypody is a winter-green, summer-dormant fern native to rocky outcrops, old walls, and streamside cliffs across western Europe and the Mediterranean, with leathery, once-pinnate fronds that are more coarsely cut than common polypody. Its unusual growth cycle runs opposite most garden ferns: new fronds unfurl in autumn, stay green through winter, and the plant goes dormant and loses its fronds during the heat of summer, so bare patches in midsummer are normal rather than a sign of trouble. It spreads slowly by a creeping, scaly rhizome that clings to rock and masonry rather than rooting deeply in soil, making it best suited to rock gardens, dry stone walls, and tufa rather than ordinary shaded borders. The wild species remains a useful, undemanding fern for lean, well-drained, shaded sites, distinct from the historic crested 'Richard Kayse' selection.

planting.note: Plant divisions in thin, humus-rich soil pockets on or around sandstone or granite boulders in partial to full shade; like other rock polypodies it resents being buried in deep garden soil and performs best where its rhizome can creep across exposed rock.

directions: Appalachian polypody is a small, evergreen native fern of the eastern mountains, forming low mats of leathery, once-pinnate fronds over moss-covered boulders and rock outcrops from the Appalachians west into the Ozarks and Interior Highlands. It was distinguished from the more widespread rock polypody, Polypodium virginianum, on the basis of chromosome number, and the two look nearly identical in the garden, sharing the same creeping, scaly rhizome and tolerance for thin, rocky soil. It thrives where little else will grow, colonizing bare rock faces and boulder tops in dappled shade, and makes a useful small-scale groundcover for rock gardens built with sandstone or other acidic stone. Give it lean soil and sharp drainage rather than rich, moist garden conditions, which encourage rot more than growth.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in deep shade; like its relatives it spreads by a slender creeping rhizome and dislikes drying out between waterings.

directions: Oyama fern is an East Asian relative of the familiar oak ferns, found in moist mountain forests from Japan south through Taiwan and the Philippines, with broader, less finely divided fronds than Gymnocarpium dryopteris and a creeping rhizome that gradually forms loose colonies. It is rarely offered commercially and remains mostly a plant for fern specialists and botanical garden collections rather than a mainstream nursery item, but where obtainable it performs much like other oak ferns, wanting cool, consistently moist, humus-rich soil and deep shade. Its deciduous fronds emerge pale green in spring and brown back with the first hard frosts, leaving the thin rhizomes to overwinter just below the soil surface. Best used as a textural groundcover among other shade-loving woodland ferns rather than as a focal specimen.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in gritty, fast-draining soil tucked into rock crevices or at the base of boulders in partial to full shade; native to shaded canyon walls and cliff faces, it does poorly in heavy or constantly wet soil.

directions: Plummer's cliff fern is a small, drought-tolerant native of shaded canyons and rocky slopes across the southwestern United States and northern Mexico, forming dense tufts of narrow, once- to twice-pinnate fronds covered in fine hairs and scales that help it survive the dry, exposed rock habitats where it typically grows. Unlike many woodland ferns it goes dormant and browns back during extended drought or hard freezes, then resprouts readily from its persistent rhizome once moisture returns, a trait shared with other dryland woodsias. It is well suited to crevice gardens, dry shaded rockeries, and xeric native plant collections where soil is thin and fast-draining rather than rich borders or consistently moist beds. Give it morning sun or filtered shade and avoid summer overhead watering, which can rot the crowns in humid climates.
